claims.text: The initial nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equiatomic ratios and form a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Stability of equiatomic multimetal nanoparticles across 473–1923 K is governed by the interplay of configurational entropy and suppressed atomic diffusion.
High configurational entropy lowers the free energy of chemically disordered solid-solution phases, particularly at high temperature.
Moderate atomic-size differences produce lattice distortion and high kinetic barriers.
Lattice distortion slows atomic migration at elevated temperatures.
Similar diffusion rates among the constituent metals create energy barriers that suppress atomic rearrangement.
When diffusion barriers are sufficient, suppressed atomic rearrangement preserves phase homogeneity.
A metal may diffuse substantially faster because of a larger atomic-size mismatch.
Unfavorable mixing enthalpy can permit ordering or secondary-phase formation to compete with entropy stabilization.
Significant differences in constituent diffusion kinetics can locally overcome entropy stabilization.
Local overcoming of entropy stabilization leads to phase segregation or secondary-phase formation.
Nanoparticles whose constituent metals have similar diffusion behavior and moderate size differences will retain a uniform single-phase structure during the specified thermal treatment.
Nanoparticles with pronounced diffusion-rate differences or larger atomic-size mismatches will develop detectable phase segregation.
Retention of a uniform single phase will maintain catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Phase segregation will degrade catalytic or thermoelectric performance relative to the initial state.
Reactive species such as aggressive oxidants can independently drive phase changes.
Two nanoparticle sets selected for contrasting diffusion kinetics and size mismatch will be subjected to identical thermal and atmospheric protocols.

The hypothesis is falsified if the similar-diffusion set segregates or loses performance, or if the pronounced-diffusion-difference set remains single-phase with unimpaired performance throughout the range.
